item.title: Door Hardware Wholesale to Abuja: Estate and Project Supply
item.description:
The short version

Abuja does not buy the way Onitsha buys. There is no carton-by-carton market rhythm here; there are estates, government buildings and hotels, and they buy against a door schedule with a specification attached.

That changes what a supplier has to do: match finishes, supply the whole door package, and be able to answer a consultant’s question about grade.

What Abuja projects specify

  • SS304 lever handles in satin or polished finish, matched across the building.
  • Mortise lock sets rather than loose locks, so the hardware arrives as a unit.
  • Concealed or SS304 butt hinges, depending on the door type.
  • Door closers on corridor and fire doors.
  • Accessories as a set — stoppers, viewers, numerals — in the same finish family.

Finish consistency is the detail that decides whether a project looks finished or assembled. It is also the reason a project order is quoted as a package, not line by line.

item.title: Door Hardware Wholesale to Kano and Northern Nigeria
item.description:
The short version

Kano is the distribution centre for northern Nigeria and it behaves differently from Lagos in one important way: the climate is kind to hardware. Dry air means galvanised steel lasts years, and the whole specification can drop a grade without the buyer paying for it later.

Logistics are the trade-off. There is no seaport in the north: containers arrive at Lagos or Onne and truck north for 2-3 days.

item.title: Door Hardware Wholesale to Lagos: Prices, Ports, Transit
item.description:
The short version

Lagos is the entry point for most Nigerian hardware imports: containers arrive at Apapa or Tin Can, clear, and then move inland by truck. Sea transit from Ningbo or Yiwu runs 25-35 days, production 15-25 days, so plan on 45-60 days from deposit to goods in your warehouse.

What sells in Lagos is driven by two things: the construction corridor and the climate.

What actually moves in Lagos

  • Iron plate mortise locks — the standard fit for Nigerian security doors. $2.50-$5.00 per piece FOB.
  • 4x3 inch butt hinges — every door takes three. SS304 for anything near the coast.
  • 50-70mm padlocks — household gates, shop shutters, motorcycles.
  • Stainless lever handles — mid-market housing and apartment projects.
  • Drawer slides and cabinet hardware — furniture workshops supplying Lekki and Ikeja estates.

Lekki, Ajah, Ikeja and the mainland corridors all build with the same door format, which is why one container mix can serve several wholesalers.

item.title: Door Hardware Wholesale to Onitsha and Ogidi Market
item.description:
The short version

Onitsha is where southeast Nigeria buys hardware. The Building Materials International Market at Ogidi, a few minutes from the city, is the reference point: shop after shop selling locks, hinges, handles, tiles, pipes and furniture fittings, mostly in cartons, mostly to traders who then supply Anambra, Enugu, Abia, Ebonyi and beyond.

Two shipping options serve it:

  • Lagos (Apapa / Tin Can) → truck east. 25-35 days at sea, then the inland leg.
  • Onne → truck north. 30-40 days at sea, shorter road leg, often the better choice for a full container.

item.title: Door Hardware Wholesale to Port Harcourt via Onne Port
item.description:
The short version

Port Harcourt has its own port. Onne takes containers in 30-40 days from Ningbo or Yiwu, and clearing there avoids the 8-10 hour Lagos truck leg entirely. For a buyer supplying Rivers, Bayelsa, Akwa Ibom and Cross River, that is usually the better route.

The climate is the other half of the story. The Niger Delta has some of the highest humidity and rainfall in Nigeria, plus salt air. Hardware that survives Kano will fail here.
